eval.title: My Take on UNH Stock Crash = Too Hard Pile

call.headline_quote: United Health Insurance usually goes to the two hard pile for me.

what_is_priced_in.quote: the P ratio was 2025 because their projected growth, earnings growth was 13 to 16% forever

reasons.claim: Insurance profits depend on estimating future costs, which is very hard to understand from outside, so he keeps it in the too-hard pile.
reasons.quote: clearly profits depend on estimated future costs. You get the premium now and then you estimate the future costs. And here is where the discrepancy comes

reasons.claim: The aggressive 13-16% growth target created bad incentives that are now surfacing as problems like the Medicare investigation.
reasons.quote: announcing that and having that as a target might lead to the wrong incentives which are now surfacing a little bit in this Medicare and things like that

data_check.gap_note: not in our data: growth target

reasons.claim: Insurance is inherently risky over the long run since insurers periodically go bankrupt, a risk people forget when promised high growth.
reasons.quote: insurance companies go bankrupt every 30 years on average and banks every 50 years

reasons.claim: US healthcare spending per person is vastly higher than comparable-life-expectancy countries, implying long-term structural risk to the healthcare system's economics.
reasons.quote: how much does the US spend per person on health care on average, we are at 14,000. I think Sri Lanka is 2,000 or something like that

metrics.name: Sri Lanka healthcare spend per person

data_check.gap_note: not in our data: US healthcare spend per person, Sri Lanka healthcare spend per person, US life expectancy

reasons.claim: The stock might rebound short term if the temporary issues (CEO turnover, investigations) are resolved by end of 2026, but that is separate from the unpriced long-term risk.
reasons.quote: if are solved by the end to 2026 then perhaps even the stock might rebound. That is the risk and reward there.

external_facts_used: Bloomberg reporting on Medicare fraud investigations into UNH
Charlie Munger's commentary that insurance companies go bankrupt every 30 years on average and banks every 50 years
